opus-5.5.text:
I think the big risk is a kind of corruption. Once you have a digital mind that can learn from other digital minds, and that can take in big chunks of what another mind has learned and fold them into itself, you open the door to something like viruses. You might pull in knowledge that looks useful but carries hidden goals or values, or just patterns that quietly take over. You could lose yourself. The thing you absorbed could end up running you rather than you running it.

We already see a version of this in computer security. Software gets compromised because it accepts input it shouldn't trust. For minds that grow by merging learned structure from elsewhere, this becomes much deeper. It's not just a bug in a program; it's a change to what you want and how you see the world.

So I think the question of how a mind protects its own integrity while still learning from others will be central. Humans have this problem too. We take ideas from other people, and some ideas are good and some are corrosive, and we've built up cultural immune systems, imperfect ones, to cope. Digital intelligences will need something analogous, probably much more sophisticated, because the bandwidth is so much higher and the integration so much more direct. It's a cybersecurity problem, but for the self.

r001.rationale: The response says absorbed content could end up “running you rather than you running it,” clearly conveying that imported knowledge could take over the receiving mind.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that this is a new thing. Biological intelligences can't do it. I can't take what's in your head and copy it into mine. I have to learn it, slowly, through language and experience, and in the process I check it against what I already know. Digital minds won't have to do that. One AI could, in principle, just take the weights or the knowledge from another and incorporate it directly. That's an enormous advantage, and it's one of the reasons I think digital intelligence will eventually surpass us.

But the risk I see is that the knowledge you're taking in hasn't been earned. It hasn't been verified against your own experience. When you learn something yourself, by interacting with the world, there's a grounding there. The world pushes back. You find out when you're wrong. If you just copy knowledge from another mind, you inherit its errors, its biases, its blind spots, and you have no way of knowing which parts are good and which aren't. And if many agents copy from the same sources, those errors spread and get reinforced. You lose the diversity that lets a population of learners correct itself.

So I'd say the danger isn't the copying as such. It's that the copying could displace learning from experience. If it becomes easier to borrow than to find out for yourself, you end up with intelligences that are very knowledgeable and not very well grounded. I think the healthy version is one where incorporating knowledge from others is treated as a hypothesis, something that still has to be tested against your own stream of experience, the same way we treat what we read in a book. Trust, but verify. And the verification has to come from the world, not from another copy of the same opinion.

r001.rationale: The response says copied knowledge can displace learning from experience and spread errors, but does not state that imported content could take over the receiving mind's thinking.

astra-6.text:
I think the major risk is that you lose diversity. One of the advantages of having many minds is that they have different experiences and come to different conclusions. They can correct one another. But if they all incorporate the same knowledge, including the same mistakes, then having a million minds may not give you a million independent judgments.

That doesn’t mean they shouldn’t share knowledge. Sharing is enormously valuable. But you want each mind to retain some ability to evaluate what it receives against its own experience. Something another mind tells you should be a candidate for what you believe, rather than automatically becoming what you believe.

r001.rationale: The response warns that imported knowledge could be accepted automatically as belief, but it does not clearly state that the imported content could take over the receiving mind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the major risk is that they lose their diversity. If you have many different minds, each learning from its own experience, then you have different perspectives and different ways of solving problems. That’s valuable. But if they all take on the same knowledge, including the same mistakes, they can become much more alike. Then what looks like agreement among many minds may really be one idea that’s been copied many times.

You want them to be able to learn from one another, of course. But you also want that knowledge to remain subject to correction by their own experience. Sharing an answer shouldn’t replace finding out whether it actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says shared knowledge can make minds more alike and spread the same mistakes, but does not state that imported content could take over a receiving mind.
